title: Normalization quotient is supported at singular points
statement:
Let $k$ be an algebraically closed field [def-weil-algebraic-closure] and $X$ a reduced finite-type $k$-scheme [def-pc-reduced-scheme, def-weil-finite-type-morphism] all of whose irreducible components have dimension one [def-weil-irreducible-components, def-kun-topological-krull-dimension]. Let $
u:X^
u	o X$ be its componentwise normalization [def-weil-pbc-reduced-normalization], and let $S$ be the set of points at which $X	o\operatorname{Spec}k$ is not smooth [def-sbc-smooth-morphisms]. Then $S$ is a finite set of closed points, each with residue field $k$ via the structural map, $
u$ is finite [def-weil-finite-integral-morphism], and there is a short exact sequence of coherent $\mathcal O_X$-modules [pqf-def-coherent]
$$0\longrightarrow\mathcal O_X\longrightarrow
u_*\mathcal O_{X^
u}\longrightarrow Q\longrightarrow0,$$
where $Q\cong igoplus_{x\in S}\mathscr S_x(M_x)$. Here $A_x=\mathcal O_{X,x}$, $C_x=(
u_*\mathcal O_{X^
u})_x$ is the integral closure [def-weil-pbc-integral-closure] of $A_x$ in its total ring of fractions (the localization obtained by inverting all non-zero-divisors), $M_x=C_x/A_x$ is a nonzero finite-length $A_x$-module (it admits a finite filtration with simple successive quotients), and $\mathscr S_x(M_x)(U)=M_x$ if $x\in U$, and $0$ otherwise, with $\mathcal O_X(U)$ acting by germs in $A_x$. Writing $\mathfrak m_x$ for the maximal ideal of $A_x$, the completions [def-weil-pbc-adic-completion]
$$\widehat A_x=\varprojlim_n A_x/\mathfrak m_x^n,\qquad \widehat C_x=\varprojlim_n C_x/\mathfrak m_x^nC_x$$
have the following properties: $\widehat C_x$ is the integral closure of $\widehat A_x$ in its total ring of fractions, and the natural map induces an $A_x$-linear isomorphism $M_x\cong\widehat C_x/\widehat A_x$.

source.place: Tag 0C1R (lemma-prepare-delta-invariant), parts (1)--(4), (7), (9), specialized to reduced finite-type curves over an algebraically closed field; finite singular support follows from Noetherian quasi-compactness. Smooth and regular loci agree over this perfect field.

proof.text:
The empty scheme satisfies the assertions with $S=\varnothing$ and $Q=0$; hence suppose $X
e\varnothing$. A field is Noetherian (its only ideals are $0$ and itself), so the finite-type-over-Noetherian lemma makes $X$ Noetherian. Apply the reduced-algebraic-normalization lemma to precisely the componentwise normalization in the statement: $
u$ is finite and surjective, the normal locus $N$ (points with integrally closed domain local ring) is dense open, $
u^{-1}N	o N$ is an isomorphism, and normalization restricts to every open. None of these assertions requires separatedness. The Noetherian finite-component lemma gives finitely many components of $X$.

Fix a nonempty affine open $U=\operatorname{Spec}R\subset X$ and write $T=\Gamma(
u^{-1}U,\mathcal O)$. By restriction of normalization and its componentwise definition, $
u^{-1}U$ is the finite disjoint union of the function-field normalizations of $\operatorname{Spec}(R/\mathfrak p_i)$, where $\mathfrak p_i$ are the minimal primes of $R$. The definition of function-field normalization and the affine description in the relative-normalization lemma identify $T=\prod_i B_i$, where $B_i$ is the integral closure of $R/\mathfrak p_i$ in $K_i=\operatorname{Frac}(R/\mathfrak p_i)$. The reduced-Noetherian total-fractions lemma identifies $Q(R)=\prod_iK_i$ (the kernel of $R	o R_{\mathfrak p_i}$ is $\mathfrak p_i$, by the localization criterion for zero). Thus $R	o T\subset Q(R)$ is injective. Because $
u$ is finite, $T$ is finite over $R$, so every element of $T$ is integral over $R$. Conversely an element of $Q(R)$ integral over $R$ has each coordinate integral over $R/\mathfrak p_i$, hence in $B_i$. Therefore $T$ is exactly the integral closure of $R$ in $Q(R)$.

source.place: Tags 0CDV (lemma-normalization-in-terms-of-components), 035F and 035H (affine integral-closure construction); varieties Tag 0C1R(3)

proof.text: For $x\in U$ corresponding to $\mathfrak p\subset R$, the affine-open stalk lemma gives $A_x=R_{\mathfrak p}$. This is reduced and Noetherian; Noetherianity follows from the localization-Noetherian lemma, and reducedness follows by clearing a denominator in a nilpotence equation. Since a finite morphism is affine, the affine-pushforward stalk lemma gives $C_x=(R\setminus\mathfrak p)^{-1}T$. Apply integral-closure localization to Step 2. Its ambient algebra $(R\setminus\mathfrak p)^{-1}Q(R)$ is $Q(R_{\mathfrak p})$: in the finite product of fields of Step 2 a factor for $\mathfrak p_i\not\subseteq\mathfrak p$ vanishes, since an element of $\mathfrak p_i\setminus\mathfrak p$ becomes invertible and is zero in that factor; every other factor is unchanged. The surviving primes $\mathfrak p_iR_{\mathfrak p}$ are exactly the minimal primes of $R_{\mathfrak p}$, and their fraction fields remain $K_i$. The total-fractions lemma applied to $R_{\mathfrak p}$ gives precisely this same product. Consequently $C_x$ is the integral closure of $A_x$ in its total ring of fractions, with the structural inclusion $A_x\hookrightarrow C_x$. It is finite over $A_x$: localize finite generators of $T$ over $R$.

The affine injections $R\hookrightarrow T$ of Step 2 imply that $\mathcal O_X	o
u_*\mathcal O_{X^
u}$ is a monomorphism: a section in its kernel restricts to zero on every affine open and hence is zero by the sheaf axiom. Both $X$ and $X^
u$ are locally Noetherian, the latter being finite type over $k$ since $
u$ is finite. On a locally Noetherian scheme the structure sheaf is coherent by the coherent/quasi-coherent-finite-type criterion. Finite pushforward therefore makes $
u_*\mathcal O_{X^
u}$ coherent. Let $Q$ be the sheaf cokernel. Coherence of cokernels gives coherence of $Q$, and stalk exactness identifies $Q_x=C_x/A_x$ and supplies the stated short exact sequence. In particular every $Q_x$ is finite over $A_x$, since the images of the localized finite generators of $C_x$ generate it.

source.place: Tag 0C1R(1)--(4); coherent.tex Tags 01XZ and 01Y6; modules.tex Tag 01BY

proof.text: For each $x$, Step 3 says $Q_x=0$ if and only if $A_x$ is integrally closed in $Q(A_x)$. Apply the reduced-normal/total-fractions equivalence: $A_x$ is reduced Noetherian and has finitely many minimal primes. It says this happens if and only if $A_x$ is normal, which for a local ring means a normal domain. Indeed in its finite product of normal domains a local nonzero ring has only one nonzero factor, because an idempotent $e$ in a local ring satisfies $e=0$ or $1$ (one of $e,1-e$ is a unit). Thus $\operatorname{Supp}Q=X\setminus N$, a closed subset. At any generic point of a component the reduced-Noetherian total-fractions lemma says the local ring is a field, so no generic point lies in this support. Since $X$ has dimension one, every irreducible closed subset of the support is a singleton closed point: otherwise it would lie strictly inside a component of $X$ and itself contain a nonempty proper irreducible closed subset, giving a chain of length two. The Noetherian closed-subset finite-component lemma now implies that $\operatorname{Supp}Q$ is a finite set of closed points.

Every closed point $x$ of $X$ has $\dim A_x=1$. In fact primes of $A_x$ correspond to generizations of $x$ in an affine neighbourhood, so the dimension is at most one; a component through $x$ has dimension one by hypothesis and cannot have $x$ as its generic point, because $x$ is closed, so its generic point gives a strict chain to $x$ of length one. The structural residue-field lemma gives $\kappa(x)=k$ as $k$-algebras. Hence that residue extension is separable, and the regular-local/separable-residue smoothness criterion gives: $X\to\operatorname{Spec}k$ is smooth at $x$ if and only if $A_x$ is regular. The dimension-one regular/normal equivalence identifies this with $x\in N$. There are no remaining nonsmooth points on $N$: all its local rings are normal domains of dimension at most one, so are fields in dimension zero and regular by the same equivalence in dimension one. Thus $N$ is regular. The algebraically closed field $k$ is perfect, and regularity over a perfect field implies smoothness on $N$. Together with Step 5 this proves $S=X\setminus N=\operatorname{Supp}Q$, including its finiteness, closedness and the asserted structural residue fields.

source.place: Tag 0C1R(2); Tag 0B8X (regular and smooth loci over a perfect field); Algebra Tags 00TV and 00PD

proof.text: For $x\in S$, put $M_x=Q_x=C_x/A_x$. It is finite and nonzero by Steps 4--6. Every nonmaximal prime of the one-dimensional local ring $A_x$ is minimal: a strictly smaller prime would give a chain of length two ending at the maximal ideal. At such a prime, localization of $Q_x$ is the stalk of $Q$ at the corresponding generic point, hence zero by Step 5. Here stalks of quasi-coherent modules are their module localizations, by the tilde-stalk lemma and an affine quasi-coherent presentation. Thus $M_x$ is supported only at the maximal ideal. The finite-module-supported-at-a-point lemma gives finite length, and the finite-length filtration lemma gives a finite filtration with simple successive quotients, as required by the statement's explicit meaning of finite length.

Use the skyscraper-stalk adjunction with the identity of $Q_x=M_x$ to obtain $Q\to\mathscr S_x(M_x)$ for each $x\in S$; on an open containing $x$ this map sends a section to its germ. Assemble them into $g:Q\to\bigoplus_{x\in S}\mathscr S_x(M_x)$, using that $S$ is finite, so direct sum equals product. The stalk of $\mathscr S_x(M_x)$ at $x$ is $M_x$, since all its neighbourhood restriction maps are identities. At $y\ne x$ it is zero: $X\setminus\{x\}$ is a neighbourhood of $y$ on which this sheaf vanishes. Taking a stalk commutes with this finite sum directly by representing finitely many germs on a common neighbourhood. Consequently $g_y$ is the identity of $M_y$ when $y\in S$, and is the map $0\to0$ otherwise. The stalkwise isomorphism criterion proves that $g$ is an isomorphism of $\mathcal O_X$-modules, with precisely the germ action and sections stipulated in the statement.

Fix $x\in S$. The affine description $A_x=R_{\mathfrak p}$ makes it a local algebra essentially of finite type over $k$; Steps 3 and 6 show reducedness and dimension one. Apply the existing curve-normalization/completion lemma with $B=C_x$, whose integral-closure description was proved in Step 3. It identifies $C_x\otimes_{A_x}\widehat A_x$ with the integral closure of $\widehat A_x$ in its total ring of fractions. Apply the finite-module completion/tensor lemma to the finite $A_x$-module $C_x$ and ideal $\mathfrak m_x$. It identifies $\widehat C_x$ with $\widehat A_x\otimes_{A_x}C_x$. Composing the tensor flip with these canonical maps identifies $\widehat C_x$ with that same integral closure. This identification respects multiplication and the map from $\widehat A_x$: on pure tensors the completion map is $a\otimes c\mapsto a\,\iota(c)$, and the product of two such images is $aa'\iota(cc')$.

source.place: Tag 0C3V (lemma-normalization-same-after-completion), completion clause; Tag 0C1R(7); Algebra Tag 00MA

proof.text: Let $r$ be the length of the simple filtration of $M_x$ in Step 7. Every simple module over the local ring $A_x$ is killed by $\mathfrak m_x$: a nonzero vector generates it, so it is $A_x/J$ with $J$ maximal, and the unique maximal ideal is $\mathfrak m_x$. Multiplication by $\mathfrak m_x$ therefore sends each stage of that filtration into the preceding stage. Iterating gives $\mathfrak m_x^rM_x=0$. For $n\ge r$ the quotients $M_x/\mathfrak m_x^nM_x$ are $M_x$ and their transition maps are identities. A compatible sequence is uniquely specified by this constant tail, its earlier terms being the reductions of the tail value. Thus the canonical completion map $M_x\to\widehat M_x$ is an $A_x$-linear isomorphism.

source.place: Tag 0C1R(9), finite-length quotient in the proof; explicit filtration argument

proof.text: Apply exactness of completion to the short exact sequence $0\to A_x\to C_x\to M_x\to0$ of finite modules over the Noetherian ring $A_x$, completing with respect to $\mathfrak m_x$. It gives $0\to\widehat A_x\to\widehat C_x\to\widehat M_x\to0$. Hence the completed quotient map induces an $A_x$-linear isomorphism $\widehat C_x/\widehat A_x\to\widehat M_x$. The map $M_x\to\widehat C_x/\widehat A_x$ induced by $c\mapsto\iota_{C_x}(c)$ is well defined, since elements of $A_x$ map into $\widehat A_x$. Its composite with this quotient isomorphism is exactly $M_x\to\widehat M_x$, by the componentwise formula for completing the quotient map. Step 10 says that composite is an isomorphism, so the natural map $M_x\to\widehat C_x/\widehat A_x$ is an isomorphism as asserted.
